justification.maxKeyedRequests: 402 = 2 x (6 enumeration + 195 candidates), the ONE-RETRY WORST CASE OF THE PLAN — captain decision 267a, 2026-08-05. IT IS NO LONGER AN ALLOWANCE FIGURE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE CHANGE: it was 200, the entire Free-tier day, and the day is now 100,000 and EXCLUSIVE to slot-zero (x-ratelimit-limit read off the wire 2026-08-05, see this block's $comment). An allowance-derived per-run ceiling would now sit four orders of magnitude above any plan and refuse nothing, and this file's standing rule is that a bound which cannot refuse is not a bound. So the value is derived from what a run can actually ISSUE instead. THE ARITHMETIC: enumeration costs 6 requests, not 3, since captain decision 262a made the seeding TIERED by default (seed.mjs -> DEFAULT_TIERS, one pass of recent-bonds/alerts/leaderboard per tier for `good` and `elite`), and the gate costs 1 per candidate, so a plan at the 195-candidate cap DECLARES 201 (screen.mjs -> worstCaseKeyed, which counts first attempts). THE FACTOR OF 2 IS THE RETRY RULE MADE EXPLICIT: a keyed request is retried at most once on a 429/5xx/transport failure and EVERY ATTEMPT counts against this ceiling (client.mjs, maxRetriesPerRequest default 1), so 402 is the most requests a plan the tool ADMITTED can actually issue, and this ceiling can therefore never stop a run it already agreed to start. THE OLD 2-REQUEST HEADROOM COULD NOT PROMISE THAT: at 200 against a 198-request worst case, three transport failures near the end of a full run breached it, and the 2 was never a statement about retries — it was simply what the allowance left. NOTE THE FORCED HALF, so this does not read as an optional widening: at the old 200 a default plan now costs 6 + 195 = 201 and would be REFUSED BEFORE ITS FIRST REQUEST, so this value had to move the moment the seeding became tiered. A run whose PLANNED worst case exceeds this is still refused before its first request rather than allowed to die part-way through. STAGE 2 ADDS NOTHING TO THIS: it reuses the profile Stage 1 already fetched and spends no keyed request of its own. WHAT ONE RUN NOW COSTS THE DAY: 201 of 100,000 is 0.201%, or 0.402% at this ceiling — roughly 248 full-cap runs a day. Nothing here tracks the day across runs, so that arithmetic stays the operator's.
justification.maxCandidates: 195, UNCHANGED IN VALUE AND COMPLETELY RE-DERIVED — captain decision 267a, 2026-08-05. SAY THE COINCIDENCE OUT LOUD, because a reader seeing the same integer will assume nothing moved: it WAS `200 - 3 enumeration - 2 retry headroom`, i.e. what the MadeOnSol day left over, and that derivation is now void — the day is 100,000 and exclusive, which would license a cap of tens of thousands and mean nothing. Two different arithmetics landing on 195 is a coincidence of integers, not continuity, and the old sentence must not be quoted for it. THE VALUE IS NOW THE LARGEST CAP THAT FITS THE CEILINGS ALREADY PINNED WITHOUT MOVING A SECOND THRESHOLD, which is the principle stage2_entry.justification.maxCandidatesScored derives 7 from. Three bounds apply and the tightest wins. (1) THE KEYLESS FRONTEND-API-V3 CEILING, WHICH BINDS: maxKeylessRequests is 1,400 with 35 of retry headroom, and a candidate costs up to 4 gate listing pages plus 3 --consistency pages = 7, so floor(1,365 / 7) = 195 EXACTLY. Above it a --consistency plan is refused before its first request. (2) THE HELIUS RUN CEILING: creation_walk_helius.maxCreditsPerRun 1,100,000 / maxCreditsPerCandidate 5,200 = 211.5, so 211. (3) ENUMERATION REACH: 6 queries x 50 rows = 300 rows, the most distinct wallets one plan can hand the gate at all — screen.mjs caps the page limit at 50 and seed.mjs clamps alerts to the same 50, so the vendor's 100-row alerts ceiling is never asked for (an earlier version of this entry read 50 + 100 + 50 over three queries, which overstated the reach). 195 is the minimum of the three, so RAISING IT CASCADES into two pinned ceilings, with the keyless RPC wall clock behind them — which is why 267a did not raise it, and why 'the day got 500x bigger' is not on its own a reason to. IT STILL COVERS WHAT ENUMERATION ACTUALLY SURFACES, which is the property this cap exists for: the highest distinct yield ever observed is 128 (2026-08-05, good 69 + elite 59, the two tier pools DISJOINT that day — runs/2026-08-05-seed-comparison.md), against 22 elite-only on 2026-07-29, 72 good-only on 2026-08-02 and 76 untiered on 2026-08-05. So the cap sits ~52% above the observed maximum, the DEFAULT run grades everything it surfaces, and coverage truncation stays the exception it is supposed to be. THE HEADROOM IS NOT PERMANENT: tier pools grow — the elite pool was 2.7x its 2026-07-29 size by 2026-08-05 — so a run record showing candidates AT the cap is evidence this needs re-deriving, not evidence of a busy day.
justification.keyedMinIntervalMs: 250ms, RE-MEASURED ON ULTRA RATHER THAN CARRIED ACROSS — captain decision 267a required exactly that, and the measurement RETIRED the constraint the old value existed for. IT WAS 6,500ms, justified on the vendor enforcing a ~10/minute burst limit: 'the vendor's rate limit, not our caution', which is precisely the kind of claim that has to be re-checked when the tier changes rather than inherited. MEASURED 2026-08-05 against the live Ultra key, one request in flight, on the two endpoints a run actually spends on. A pacing ladder over /deployer-hunter/leaderboard at enforced intervals of 6,500 / 2,000 / 500 / 0 ms, 12 requests a rung, recorded ZERO shed events and zero non-200 responses at EVERY RUNG INCLUDING 0 ms; then 60 back-to-back requests at 0 ms — 19.7 s, 3.05 req/s, i.e. ~183/minute sustained — also shed NOTHING, which a ~10/minute limiter would have refused at request 11. The gate's own endpoint, /deployer-hunter/{wallet}, behaved the same: 30 back-to-back, 0 shed, 4.95 req/s, and x-ratelimit-used advanced by exactly 30, so the counter is per-request and global across endpoints rather than per-endpoint. So the ~10/minute figure does not describe this tier and 6,500ms was buying nothing. WHAT BINDS INSTEAD IS RESPONSE LATENCY, exactly as on Helius: p50 312ms on the leaderboard and 182ms on the profile endpoint, so one serial client tops out near 3-5 req/s whatever the interval says. 250ms is therefore A COURTESY FLOOR AND NOT A SHED-AVOIDANCE FIGURE — the same character as creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200ms, measured the same way on a vendor that also shed nothing) and the same number this file already pins for its other keyed host in dune.minIntervalMs. It sits at or below the measured latency of both endpoints, so it costs a run essentially nothing while keeping a serial floor in place rather than none at all. THREE LIMITS ON THAT MEASUREMENT, STATED RATHER THAN GLOSSED: it is ONE DAY, on ~150 requests, so it bounds nothing about a sustained multi-hour leg; it says nothing about CONCURRENCY, because this client issues one request at a time and no probe put several in flight; and it cannot see a limiter that only bites well above 183/minute, which serial pacing structurally cannot reach. What would extend it: a rung ladder repeated across several days, and a concurrency probe of the shape creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs records. The 'margin matters because the allowance is shared' half of the old reasoning is void rather than merely weakened — the key is EXCLUSIVE since captain, 2026-08-05. THE WALL-CLOCK CONSEQUENCE IS LARGE AND IS WHAT A READER WANTS FIRST: the keyed leg of a full 201-request run goes from ABOUT 21 MINUTES to ABOUT 50 SECONDS. THAT WAS NEVER THE RUN'S WALL CLOCK AND STILL IS NOT. The default history source is creation-derived, and the Solana RPC walk dominates everything else by an order of magnitude: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s is ~13.5 HOURS on its own. Add ~50 seconds keyed, ~26 minutes for the gate's ownership listing on frontend-api-v3, ~147 for Stage 2 on swap-api (7 x 10 x 18), up to ~146 more for Stage 2's cost leg (stage2_cost, 7 x 500 requests at the same 2.5s, and it SHARES this limiter rather than adding a second queue), and a further ~19.5 with --consistency, and a full default run at the candidate cap is ABOUT 18.9 HOURS end to end, or ~19.2 with --consistency. Those two Stage 2 legs multiplied when the scoring cap went 3 -> 7 on 2026-08-04; stage2_entry.justification.maxCandidatesScored owns that raise and its cost, and this entry only carries the total. Earlier versions of this note said 47 minutes (it predated the creation walk and was wrong by a factor of twenty) and then 19.2 hours (correct while keyed pacing was 6.5s, which contributed ~21 minutes of it). DO NOT KILL A DEFAULT RUN FOR STILL GOING AFTER AN HOUR. The liveness signal is not the same on every leg: the keyed and frontend-api-v3 clients print one line per request, but the creation walk would emit ~20,000 of those, so it prints a PERIODIC HEARTBEAT — the first request of each candidate and then every tenth, i.e. a line roughly every 25 seconds at this walk's 2.5s pacing, showing that candidate's spend against maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate. Watch that counter rather than expecting a line per request, and use --candidates N to bound the run (the RPC leg is N x 100 x 2.5s) or --ownership-only to skip the walk entirely for a fast pass whose bias runs BOTH ways at once — it REJECTS through the count bars and INFLATES through the rate — and is stamped into the record as historySource: 'ownership-only'. renderDryRun prints this arithmetic for whatever flags are actually passed.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: frontend-api-v3.pump.fun — the gate's ownership listing and the --consistency creator walk, which share one client. It does NOT govern the Stage 2 fill walk, which has its own pinned pacing (`stage2_entry.keylessMinIntervalMs`) because it reaches a different host that behaves differently. THIS VALUE IS A CONSERVATIVE CARRY-OVER, NOT A MEASUREMENT OF THE ENDPOINT IT GOVERNS, and the correction matters: the ~0.5 requests/second figure this was originally justified by was measured against api.mainnet-beta.solana.com, and the June report's own spend table records BOTH swap-api.pump.fun and frontend-api-v3.pump.fun as NOT CONTACTED — so it was never a pump.fun measurement at all. It is kept because it is conservative and because frontend-api-v3 has shed nothing in this tool's use of it; if that host is ever measured, this number should be re-derived from that measurement rather than from a different host's. Either way it bounds a shared public resource rather than expressing our own caution, so the MadeOnSol relaxation does not touch it. The RETRY COUNT is a separate question and is not this bound: a keyless request is retried on a 429 or a 5xx, and each attempt counts against maxKeylessRequests.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: A PER-CLIENT CEILING, NOT A RUN TOTAL, and the distinction is what the code enforces: screen.mjs builds TWO independent keyless clients, and this value bounds only the general one (frontend-api-v3). Stage 2 runs on its own client under its own `stage2_entry.maxKeylessRequests` of 1,260, which this number neither contains nor constrains, so the enforced combined worst case is 1,400 + 1,260 = 2,660 requests (it was 1,400 + 540 = 1,940 before the proof-coverage lane raised the scoring cap to 7 on 2026-08-04, and 1,400 + 432 = 1,832 before captain decision 190a raised the launch cap to 10). 1,400 is sized to COVER the candidate cap rather than to bound it, and it is sized for what the code now actually spends on this client, which is TWO passes and not one. The GATE reads the ownership listing it merges the creation window with, up to 4 pages PER CANDIDATE (screen.mjs LISTING_PAGES_FOR_MERGE); the --consistency pass then costs up to 3 pages per gate SURVIVOR, and every candidate can be one. So 195 candidates cost 195 x 4 = 780 for the gate plus 195 x 3 = 585 for consistency = 1,365 worst case, and the remaining 35 are the retry headroom. The earlier 600 was justified on the consistency pass alone and was already exceeded by gating at the default candidate cap. SINCE CAPTAIN DECISION 267a THIS ENTRY ALSO FIXES maxCandidates, AND THE DEPENDENCY NOW RUNS THE OTHER WAY: 1,365 / 7 pages a candidate = 195 EXACTLY, which is the tightest of the three bounds on the candidate cap and therefore the one that sets it. Before 267a the keyed allowance set the cap and this ceiling was sized to COVER it; the MadeOnSol day is now 100,000 and exclusive and binds nothing, so the two swapped roles without either number moving. RAISING maxCandidates NOW REQUIRES RAISING THIS FIRST, or a --consistency plan at the new cap is refused before its first request. A keyless ceiling below the plan would make the tool stop looking part-way through a run it had already paid for in KEYED quota, and an unmeasured candidate is not a measured one — so screen.mjs now also REFUSES a plan whose keyless worst case does not fit, before its first request, exactly as it does for the keyed one. Raising the count does not lean harder on pump.fun — keylessMinIntervalMs is unchanged, so what it buys is wall-clock time and nothing else: 1,365 requests at 2s is ~45.5 minutes, of which ~26 is the gate's own 780 pages. That is a minority of the run's wall clock rather than the whole of it — see keyedMinIntervalMs, where the creation walk's ~13.5 hours puts a full default run at ABOUT 18.9 HOURS (13.54 h RPC + ~50 s keyed + ~26 min gate listing + ~147 min Stage 2 + ~146 min the cost leg = 18.87 h; Stage 2's leg was ~63 min and the cost leg ~62.5 min at the scoring cap of 3, so the proof-coverage lane's cap of 7 adds ~2.8 h to what was a 16.42-hour run. Earlier versions of this sentence said 15, contradicting the total four lines above it, and then 19.2 h, which was right while keyed pacing was 6.5s and contributed ~21 min of it — captain decision 267a's re-measured 250ms took that leg to ~50 s). The June report sustained 460 consecutive keyless requests at 1.4s apart with zero shedding. These are pump.fun's free endpoints — no key, no vendor allowance, and no shared quota is touched by any of it.

$comment: Bounds for the creation-derived launch history — the walk that answers 'which tokens did this
wallet CREATE' instead of 'which tokens does it OWN NOW'. See creation.mjs for why the two
differ and for the on-chain observation that established it.
This walk is the expensive part of a run by an order of magnitude, because the only keyless
index that reaches a create transaction is the wallet's own signature index, and for a pump.fun
deployer that index is dominated by strangers' failed trades. Every bound here is therefore a
hard ceiling, and readCreatedHistory reports which one bit rather than truncating silently.
The walk covers a CONTIGUOUS WINDOW BACKWARDS FROM NOW. Inside it every creation is found;
outside it none is, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing and says so. A
create count read as a lifetime figure under any stopReason other than 'index-exhausted' is
wrong in the same direction as the vendor's sliding 'lifetime' window.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: Measured 2026-08-02: sustained keyless throughput against api.mainnet-beta is about 0.42 transactions/second, i.e. roughly one request per 2.4s including backoff, and a create is found by inspecting every SUCCEEDED signature in the wallet's index. The success fraction varies enormously between deployers — 1.7% on the busiest wallet screened, 99.7% on another — so the cost of a full history ranged from 7 minutes to 84 hours across the 12 wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json. 100 requests is a per-candidate ceiling that keeps a 12-candidate run inside about 50 minutes; on a quiet wallet it is the whole history, on a busy one it is a window of hours and the record says so. NOTE THE OTHER END OF THAT ARITHMETIC: at the 195-candidate cap it is 19,500 requests and ~13.5 HOURS, which is the dominant cost of a default run — --candidates N is the lever that bounds it, and --ownership-only skips it for a fast pass whose bias is stamped into the record. See CREATION-DERIVED.md for the per-wallet costs.
justification.maxSignaturePages: 200 pages is 200,000 signatures, past which no keyless walk is finishing inside a session. It exists so a wallet with an enormous index cannot turn the request ceiling into the only brake.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, and there is no measurement behind the number. pumpfun.mjs stops the walk at transactionsInspected >= this, but a transaction is inspected one getTransaction at a time (txBatchSize 1) from a client capped at maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate 100, so AT MOST ~100 transactions can ever be inspected for one candidate — 8000 is unreachable by a factor of ~80, and every real walk stops on 'request-ceiling' or 'index-exhausted' instead. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising the request ceiling does not silently remove the only bound on inspection work, and it is documented as unjustified rather than given a manufactured anchor: what would justify a value is a measured cost per inspected transaction against a wall-clock budget, which only exists for the REQUEST ceiling (see maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate, 0.42 tx/s measured 2026-08-02). Delete it or re-derive it if the request ceiling ever rises above it.
justification.txBatchSize: 1, and the 1 is measured. report.md 9.4 recorded batches of 5-8 getTransaction as sustainable, and that no longer holds: on 2026-08-02, fetching the same transactions at batch=1 took 58s with ZERO load-shed events, batch=4 took 76s with 7, and batch=8 took 110s with 11. Throughput was 0.42 tx/s at batch=1 and 0.36 tx/s at batch=8 — the endpoint weights each entry of a JSON-RPC batch against its limiter, so a batch of 8 spends 8 tokens and buys nothing but backoff. Batching is therefore actively harmful HERE TOO, exactly as it is on pump.fun's keyless endpoints. The client still supports batching, capped at 8, because the endpoint's behaviour is the vendor's to change and re-measuring is cheaper than rebuilding.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: 1,400ms is the documented floor, but a 200-request run at that pace on 2026-08-02 took over 890 seconds instead of the expected 280 — the endpoint was shedding load and the retry backoff was paying for it. 2,500ms is the observed rate at which that stops happening, so it is faster in wall-clock than the nominally quicker setting. api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction, and two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout, so this is one queue with one request in flight.

$comment: CREATION ENUMERATION, PRIMARY SURFACE. Captain decision 156a, 2026-08-03. The same question
creation_walk and creation_walk_helius answer — 'which mints did this wallet CREATE' — read
off Dune's decoded pump.fun creation events instead of walked out of a signature index.
tools/deployer-screen/dune.mjs owns the method; CREATION-DERIVED.md section 8 owns the
reproduction and the measured cost.
THE SURFACE IS A UNION AND THE UNION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: pump_evt_createevent UNION
pump_call_create, deduped by mint. pump_call_create ALONE returns ZERO rows for our subject
(it decodes only the original Create; this deployer uses CreateV2). pump_call_create_v2 ALONE
is not backfilled before ~2026-04-28 and silently misses 101 of our 239 launches, `maxxing`
included. Attribution keys on "user"/account_user, the SIGNER — never on `creator`, which is
a settable CreateV2 argument that six bot-signed mints use to name our subject, inflating the
EVERY DUNE-DERIVED COUNT SHIPS WITH ITS OWN COVERAGE PROBE, and that is the binding condition
of the decision rather than a nicety. Decoded tables have SILENT START DATES: they return a
confident, well-formed, complete-looking answer that is simply wrong before their first row,
with nothing in the response saying so. Same failure shape as a truncated backwards walk in
pumpfun.mjs and the same direction: plausible and silent. dune.mjs -> assessCoverage refuses
a reading that reaches outside the probe, and a refused reading FALLS BACK to the walk — it is
never published as a measured count.
SPEND. TWO CEILINGS APPLY AND THE SMALLER BINDS (captain decision 322a). The vendor reports
what its plan includes for the current billing period — 2,500 credits when this was written —
and monthlyCreditCapCredits below is the CAPTAIN'S OWN fleet-wide monthly cap. The key is the
captain's alone and UNSHARED; the allowance is still ACCOUNT-wide, so every lane of this fleet
draws on the same total. What a run may spend against whichever ceiling binds is CHECKED
BEFORE ITS FIRST REQUEST — dune.mjs -> checkDuneAllowance, and README.md -> 'The monthly
credit ceiling' owns it — but nothing here carries state ACROSS runs. The cap binds anyway,
because it is applied to the PERIOD's own credits_used rather than to a run; what is still
the operator's is only how many runs to spend it on.
A FAILED EXECUTION IS STILL BILLED AND IS TERMINAL: client.mjs -> DuneClient never retries
one, and no code may wrap a retry around it. Budget from BILLED credits, not
execution_cost_credits, which understates by ~3.5x because retrieving results is ~71% of the
bill at ~20 credits/MB.

justification.monthlyCreditCapCredits: THE CAPTAIN'S OWN MONTHLY CEILING, IN CONFIGURATION BECAUSE THAT IS THE ONLY PLACE IT MAY LIVE. Captain decision 322a, 2026-08-06: `4,000 credits a month, and I do not want to exceed it but still use it all in a smart way`. NOT A MEASUREMENT AND NOT DERIVED FROM ONE: it is the operator's stated budget, so this entry names its source rather than an anchor. An operator changes the number HERE and in tools/creation-census/bounds.json -> dune.monthlyCreditCapCredits, which test/dune-credit-ceiling.test.ts pins equal to it because neither keyed tool may import the other. HOW IT BINDS: client.mjs -> bindingCreditCeiling takes the SMALLER of this and the vendor's reported credits_included for the current billing period, and decideAllowance measures that period's own credits_used against it — which enforces a monthly total on a tool that holds no state between runs, since the vendor's counter is the ACCOUNT's running total and not a run's. BOTH FIGURES REACH EVERY VERDICT, so a refusal says which ceiling bound and whether raising this number or waiting for the period to roll is the fix. WHY A min() AND NOT A CHOSEN NUMBER: both sides move, and this account's own figure moved while the decision was being implemented. A min() handles a plan that grows, a cap that the captain changes and a vendor figure that changes mid-period with no edit to any of it. WHAT IT ENFORCES IS PER ACCOUNT-PERIOD, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS FLEET-WIDE, AND THE GAP IS STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: the fleet holds MORE THAN ONE Dune key, separate keys are separate accounts with separate quotas and separate period boundaries, and each counter knows only its own spend — so two keys each honouring this cap spend twice it between them, with neither run wrong. Closing that needs one key or a smaller cap on each, and both are the captain's decision. DO NOT WRITE A VENDOR FIGURE OR A PERIOD DOWN HERE: measured live through this repo's own readUsage, one key reported credits_included 2500 / credits_used 2044.357 over 2026-07-29 -> 2026-08-29 (2026-08-07T01:42:32Z) while the captain reports a second key at 4000 included / 0 used over 2026-08-06 -> 2026-09-06. Read the figure and the period out of the response the key in use returned; the guard already does.
justification.creationQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved query the enumeration executes, pinned so a run names the surface it read. dune.mjs -> CREATION_SQL holds that query's SQL byte for byte and assertSavedQueryMatches compares the two BEFORE spending an execution, so a saved query edited from a browser fails the run loudly instead of returning a different measurement under the same name. Reused rather than created: it is the query `slot-zero-dune-evaluate` section 7 (held in firstmate's records, not in this repo) designates as the production shape, upgraded in place from event-only to the union, because the free tier allows only 10 private queries and the account holds 10. THEREFORE EVERY CHANGE TO CREATION_SQL IS A DEPLOY STEP AGAINST THIS QUERY ID: saved query 8204672 must be edited in place to the committed text before the next real run, because the comparison happens BEFORE the execution and a mismatch is not a wrong answer — it is a terminal refusal of the whole Dune leg on every run until they agree. There is no new query slot to create. tools/deployer-screen/README.md -> 'Deploying a change to the committed SQL' owns the step.
justification.coverageQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved coverage probe, pinned for the same reason and verified the same way against COVERAGE_SQL. It is the scout's own coverage query (report.md section 2) widened to carry min/max block time beside the monthly counts. It probes THREE tables while the enumeration reads TWO: pump_call_create_v2 is included precisely so the probe's own output demonstrates the boundary that disqualifies it, rather than this file asserting it in prose.
justification.maxExecutionsPerRun: 2, and the 2 is the exact plan rather than a round number: one execution for the enumeration, and at most one more to re-execute the coverage probe when the cached one has gone stale. Nothing else in a run may execute. An execution is BILLED WHETHER OR NOT IT SUCCEEDS and is never retried, so this is the bound on the only unrecoverable spend the Dune leg has. MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this account: the enumeration of 5 wallets / 482 rows cost 0.919 execution credits and 1.919 billed; the coverage probe cost 0.751 execution credits and 0.751 billed. AT THE 195-CANDIDATE CAP the execution cost barely moves — scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter, measured at 5 and at 20 — and what scales is bytes returned, which maxResultRows bounds. THIS BOUNDS ONE RUN, and it is what the monthly credit guard prices that run against: worstCaseCreditsPerExecution x this value is the compute half of the plan checkDuneAllowance compares with the account's remaining balance before the first request. The tool is still stateless BETWEEN runs, so the arithmetic across them stays the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxRequestsPerRun: Requests bound the WALL CLOCK and the polite use of a shared host; maxExecutionsPerRun bounds the money, and the two are separate ceilings because a poll loop that spent an execution's worth of budget on status checks would be counting the wrong thing. The arithmetic: each of the two possible executions costs 1 SQL-verification GET + 1 execute + up to maxPollAttempts 40 status polls + 1 results read = 43, so 2 x 43 = 86, plus the credit guard's single POST /usage and its one retry = 88, and the remaining 12 are the retry headroom (every read is retried at most once, and each attempt counts). 100 covers that sum. MEASURED: both executions on 2026-08-03 completed in 6-9 s, i.e. 2-3 polls, so a real run spends about 8 requests and the ceiling is a backstop rather than a budget. THE CANCEL IS THE ONE REQUEST THIS CEILING MAY NOT REFUSE and it is therefore NOT in that sum (captain decision 381): an abandonment happens with the request budget at or near its limit by construction, so a ceiling that blocked `client.mjs` -> `cancelExecution` would turn a bounded bill into an unbounded one at exactly the moment the bound is needed. It still counts as ISSUED, so a run that had to cancel reports `requests` above this ceiling rather than the counter quietly under-reporting; a successful run never sends one.
justification.maxResultRows: 40,000 rows, RAISED FROM 20,000 BY CAPTAIN DECISION 264a (2026-08-05) AFTER THE CEILING REFUSED A REAL RUN, and THE UNIT THAT MATTERS IS STILL BYTES rather than rows, because results are billed at ~20 credits/MB and that is ~71% of the bill. WHAT LEAVING IT AT 20,000 COST, which is the whole evidence for the raise: 2026-08-05, an untiered default run at 76 deployers (runs/2026-08-05-seed-comparison.md, leg A). The per-deployer cap of 500 permitted 38,000 rows, the batch returned 27,731, and the reading was refused WHOLE — dune.rowsReturned 0, dune.coverage null, enumerationSource 'helius' on all 76 candidates. That leg then spent 232,937 Helius credits and 4,105 RPC requests against 1,924 and 33 for the 69-deployer leg that KEPT its Dune answer, i.e. ~121x the credits for the same measurement; and it lost captain decision 227a's mayhem flag entirely, mayhemShare null on 76 of 76, which means UNMEASURED and never 0%, since that flag is a Dune column no walk-sourced leg can report. The refusal itself was CORRECT — an unbounded read is an unbounded bill — so what was wrong is the ceiling, not the reader. TWO BOUNDS HOLD AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT BOUNDS. (1) THE BYTES BOUND, unchanged in method and re-priced: every result read is issued with `?limit=maxResultRows`, so no read can return more rows than this whatever the query does. `?limit=40000` was VERIFIED ACCEPTED by the vendor before this value moved (HTTP 200 against the production coverage query 8204603, 2026-08-05) rather than assumed to be in range. MEASURED 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns: ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes), and RE-MEASURED 2026-08-05 at the SIX columns CREATION_SQL selects today — `launches_total`, which makes the per-deployer cap below detectable instead of silent, and `is_mayhem_mode`, captain decision 227a's recorded-and-reported flag. The six-column shape reads 105.92 bytes/row batch-shaped (51,691 bytes over 488 rows, five wallets) and 105.91 for a single wallet (26,690 over 252), so <=121 bytes/row still holds — AT 40,000 ROWS THAT IS <=~4.84 MB AND ~97 CREDITS for a read that fills this ceiling, double what it was. The per-ROW headroom on resultBytesPerRowCeiling is 15.08 bytes and is UNAFFECTED by this raise: more rows buys a seventh column no room at all, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c still owns what one must do before it is added. WHAT THE RAISE COSTS THE CREDIT GUARD, priced rather than waved at: checkDuneAllowance converts the plan as maxExecutionsPerRun x worstCaseCreditsPerExecution + (maxExecutionsPerRun + 1) reads x this value x resultBytesPerRowCeiling at 20 credits/MB, so the EXPORT half goes 3 x 20,000 x 121 B = 145.2 credits to 3 x 40,000 x 121 B = 290.4. At the worstCaseCreditsPerExecution of the day (25) that made the whole worst case 195.2 -> 340.4; CAPTAIN DECISION 381 HAS SINCE RAISED THAT PIN 25 -> 200 AND THE WHOLE WORST CASE IS NOW 2 x 200 + 290.4 = 690.4, so the figures either side of this raise are quoted at the pin that applied when it was taken and are not the live ones. At allowanceTightMultiple 2 and allowanceReserveCredits 25 a run needs 1,405.8 of the period's credits to read `sufficient` rather than `tight` — so a full-cap run still clears from a fresh period, and a period already ~72% spent warns where it used to pass. The guard still REFUSES before the first request and falls back to the RPC walk, which is the direction this leg fails in. A REAL RUN IS NOWHERE NEAR EITHER FIGURE: the three legs of 2026-08-05 read 2,937,602 / 200,869 / 282,958 result bytes, i.e. ~59 / ~4 / ~6 export credits. (2) THE ROWS BOUND, whose crossover moved WHILE THE SQL DID NOT: CREATION_SQL returns at most greatest(500, floor(19999 / <deployers in the batch>)) rows PER DEPLOYER — 500 a pinned floor, and 19,999 the value dune.mjs -> SQL_ROW_CEILING holds, both written as literals in the SQL because a saved Dune query cannot read this file, and both guarded by a test. So a run's rows are bounded at max(19,999, <deployers> x 500), which EXCEEDS THIS CEILING ABOVE 80 DEPLOYERS where it used to exceed it above 40 — and a result that does is still refused whole by the reader, exactly as before the cap existed, rather than published. It is NOT a by-construction bound and must not be quoted as one; the arithmetic a given run applies is visible in the dry run. SQL_ROW_CEILING IS DELIBERATELY LEFT AT 19,999 AND THE TWO ARE NO LONGER EQUAL. It used to be pinned at exactly this value minus one and DERIVED from it; the test now pins the INEQUALITY (SQL_ROW_CEILING <= maxResultRows - 1) instead. TWO REASONS, and the second is the operational one. (a) The equality was a DERIVATION, not the safety property. What matters is that a result honouring the derived half of the per-deployer cap can never sit ON its own `?limit=`, and 19,999 < 40,000 satisfies that more strongly than 19,999 < 20,000 did. What the frozen literal costs is that a ONE-wallet batch is still capped at 19,999 rows rather than 39,999 — which binds nothing: the largest per-wallet history this repo has measured is 247 and the industrial-spam extreme reachable from the total_bonded leaderboard is 8,518, both far under 19,999. Above 39 deployers the 500 floor binds and the share-out is not consulted at all, so the frozen literal is invisible on every batch a real run makes. (b) EDITING CREATION_SQL IS HALF A CHANGE: assertSavedQueryMatches compares the committed text against saved Dune query 8204672 BEFORE spending an execution, so a repo-side edit not deployed in place refuses the WHOLE Dune leg terminally, on every run, until they agree. Raising this ceiling by editing only this file needs no deploy and therefore cannot leave the leg refusing; re-coupling the two is a separate change that carries that deploy step and buys nothing measurable. See creationQueryId and README.md -> 'Deploying a change to the committed SQL'. WHY THE 500 FLOOR EXISTS AND WHY THIS RAISE DOES NOT TOUCH IT: a purely derived cap is 102 rows at the 195-candidate cap, which would truncate the subject deployer (247 launches, the reproduction control) and 4q4GKBpV (152) on every full run — a systematic per-wallet failure biased towards the largest and most gate-relevant wallets, which is worse than the rare all-or-nothing one it replaced. 500 is ~2x the largest per-wallet history this repo has measured (8/10/65/152/247, CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.3), so NO measured deployer is capped at any batch size, and ~17x below the industrial-spam extreme (8,518 deploys), so a spam wallet is still contained. It is pinned on its own evidence and moves only on its own. WHY THAT SECOND BOUND EXISTS AT ALL: this ceiling refuses the WHOLE RESULT, and enumeration is ONE execution for the whole batch, so before the cap a single industrial-spam deployer (README records an 8,518-deploy wallet reachable from the total_bonded leaderboard, one of the seeds) carried every other candidate past it and sent the entire run to the RPC walk — ~13 hours of walking traded against ~1 credit of Dune, decided by one outlier. The cap moves that refusal onto the wallet that earned it: a deployer whose true count exceeds its share is detected exactly (declared count above rows returned), refused with a reason, and walks alone. THE CEILING IS KEPT AS THE BACKSTOP rather than deleted, and it stays genuinely REACHABLE — preserving that is what the raise had to do rather than undo. Roughly 80 wallets of 500+ launches in one batch put a result past it, and at the shape actually measured (27,731 rows over 76 deployers = 364.9 rows/deployer) it is reached at about 109 deployers, both under the 195-candidate cap; such a run falls back whole exactly as merged main already did — never worse than today, just not eliminated. Under captain decision 262a's TIERED default the measured shape is far lighter — 1,896 rows over 69 deployers and 2,672 over 59, i.e. 27.5 and 45.3 rows a deployer — so a default run sits two orders of magnitude clear of this ceiling and the raise is insurance for a wide or untiered batch rather than a change to the normal case. Reaching it otherwise means the cap did not apply — a saved query edited past the committed text, or a shape the reader does not understand — and a soft bound on a billed read is not a bound. WHAT A REAL RUN COSTS AGAINST IT: at the 195-candidate cap and a median deployer history of ~50 launches, ~9,750 rows is ~0.95 MB, about 20 credits — roughly 125 full-cap runs a month, unchanged by this raise because a median-shaped batch never approaches either ceiling. The ceiling REFUSES rather than pages: an unbounded read is an unbounded bill, and a paged one would spend the allowance discovering how big the answer was.
justification.pollIntervalMs: 3,000 ms between status polls. MEASURED 2026-08-03: the two executions finished in 6 s and 9 s, so a run polls two or three times. Polling faster would buy at most a couple of seconds against a leg that replaces a walk measured in hours, and it is a shared free-tier host. Polling is a READ and costs no execution credit, but every poll counts against maxRequestsPerRun, which is what stops a slow execution turning into an unbounded loop.
justification.maxPollAttempts: 40 polls at 3,000 ms is 120 s, against the 6-9 s the two committed executions actually took — roughly 13x the observed worst. IT IS THE REQUEST BUDGET, NOT THE GIVE-UP POINT (captain decision 381): `dune.executionDeadlineMs` is the give-up point and is the authority, and this must COVER it — a test pins `maxPollAttempts x pollIntervalMs >= executionDeadlineMs` so the request budget can never be what silently ends the wait first. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE, and it is stated as an operational bound rather than dressed up: nothing in this repo measures the tail of Dune execution latency, because two executions is not a distribution. What would justify a value: execution durations over a month of scheduled runs, which the run record's dune block will accumulate. The failure direction is the safe one — running out of polls abandons the Dune leg and falls back to the RPC walk — but 'the execution is billed either way' USED TO END THE SENTENCE HERE AND THAT WAS THE HOLE: walking away does not stop the engine, which runs to Dune's own 30-minute limit and bills the full limit, measured at 180.002 credits. Both give-up paths now CANCEL first, so the cost of being wrong here is bounded by one execution's DEADLINE rather than by the vendor's timeout.
justification.minIntervalMs: 250 ms between request starts, and NO MEASUREMENT OF THIS HOST BACKS IT. It is a courtesy floor on a free tier, carried across from creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200 ms, which WAS measured, on a different vendor) and rounded up rather than down. A real run issues about 8 requests, so the pacing costs ~2 s of a run measured in minutes and buying a measurement of it would be spending a shared allowance to tune something that is not a cost. What would justify a value: a pacing ladder against Dune's status endpoint recording shed events per rung, which is exactly what was done for Helius and has not been done here.
justification.maxCoverageLagMs: 6 hours. The probe cannot vouch for a period it does not reach, and the recent end is precisely where a live screen looks — a deployer that launched this morning is the one a discovery feed just surfaced. Dune's own freshness was measured by the scout at ~3-4 minutes (report.md section 6, item 8), so 6 hours is about 100x the vendor's lag and is not a tight bar; what it actually bounds is OUR cache, since the probe defaults to a cached read that could be arbitrarily old. THE FAILURE IS REPAIRED RATHER THAN INHERITED: when staleness is the ONLY thing wrong, dune.mjs re-executes the probe once, which is the second of the two budgeted executions. A structural refusal — a missing table, a month with no rows — is not retried, because asking the same question again returns the same answer.
justification.worstCaseCreditsPerExecution: 200 credits, RAISED FROM 25 BY CAPTAIN DECISION 381 (2026-08-08) AND RE-DERIVED AGAINST THE ENGINE TIMEOUT RATHER THAN AGAINST THESE TWO STATEMENTS. It is the WORST case one of this leg's executions may cost, and the input the monthly-ceiling guard converts a plan into money with (client.mjs -> estimatePlanCredits). WHY THE OLD DERIVATION WAS THE WRONG QUANTITY: it priced what CREATION_SQL and COVERAGE_SQL cost when they work. MEASURED on this account, 2026-08-03, for THESE two queries: the enumeration 0.919 execution credits and the coverage probe 0.751, and scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter (measured at 5 and at 20). The widest execution any slot-zero lane had recorded that does NOT join the trade tape was 19.25 credits (a curated-schema table listing, `slot-zero-launch-venue-daily-rates` section 7, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo); the two that DID join `dex_solana.trades` cost 81.74 and 221.51. All of that is still true and none of it BOUNDS anything: a statement that degrades does not cost a little more, it runs until Dune's engine kills it. MEASURED 2026-08-08: a statement that compiled, ran to the 30-minute engine limit, returned no rows and ended QUERY_STATE_FAILED billed 180.002 credits, read off the free POST /usage counter either side with no other execution in flight (219.825 -> 399.827) and re-read after settling (`slot-zero-venue-gradeability-inventory` -> report.md section 0, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo). The guard cleared the plan that did it at a pinned 6, printing `verdict: sufficient`. SO THE NUMBER IS DERIVED FROM THE VENDOR'S CEILING, NOT FROM OUR STATEMENTS: client.mjs -> executionDeadlineCredits(ENGINE_TIMEOUT_MS) is 181 credits (180.002 rounded up to whole credits, the granularity the vendor's counter advances in), and 200 is that plus ~10% because the reading is n=1 on one engine size against a vendor that publishes no rate. A test pins this value at or above that floor and pins it EQUAL to the census's, because a floor that binds one keyed lane is not a floor. WHAT IT DOES TO THIS LEG'S PLANNING: the worst case goes 340.4 -> 690.4 credits (2 executions at 200, plus 3 reads x 40,000 rows x 121 B = 290.4 export). Against the 4,000-credit cap a run is REFUSED once the period's credits_used passes ~3,285 where it used to pass ~3,635, and reads `tight` rather than `sufficient` above ~2,594; on a key whose vendor plan is 2,500 the refusal moves to ~1,785. THE FAILURE DIRECTION IS UNCHANGED AND IS THE SAFE ONE - a refused Dune leg falls back to the Solana RPC walk, which is slower rather than wrong - but it is NOT free: `dune.legFallbackCliffMultiple` exists because a whole-leg fallback is a Helius spend cliff, so a period spent past ~82% now buys the walk. A REAL RUN IS NOWHERE NEAR EITHER FIGURE (the three legs of 2026-08-05 read ~59 / ~4 / ~6 export credits), so what the raise costs is HEADROOM RESERVED rather than credits spent. THE PIN IS ONLY HALF THE ANSWER: `dune.executionDeadlineMs` is what actually caps a single execution, and a pin without the deadline reserves the money without bounding the spend. NEITHER QUERY MAY GROW A TRADE JOIN WITHOUT RE-MEASURING THIS NUMBER: CREATION_SQL and COVERAGE_SQL read the decoded create surfaces only, and the trade-join figures above were SUCCESSFUL executions that say nothing about where a joined statement's own timeout floor sits.
justification.executionDeadlineMs: 120,000 ms - how long ONE execution may run before this client CANCELS it, captain decision 381 (2026-08-08). It is the half of that decision that bounds a spend rather than reserving against it: a pre-flight allowance check cannot cap an execution, because the spend happens after the check passes and Dune caps a single execution's cost nowhere. THE VALUE MOVES NOTHING TODAY AND THAT IS DELIBERATE: 120,000 is exactly `maxPollAttempts` 40 x `pollIntervalMs` 3,000, i.e. the give-up point dune.mjs -> executeAndRead already had. What changes is what giving up MEANS - the loop now issues POST /execution/{id}/cancel before it refuses, where it used to walk away and leave the engine running on our money to the vendor's 30-minute limit. That is the measured failure: 180.002 credits for a result nobody read. THE TWO NUMBERS ARE ONE BOUND IN TWO UNITS AND THIS ONE IS THE AUTHORITY, which is captain decision 144a's rule (never write two numbers for a duration someone else controls); test/dune-credit-ceiling.test.ts pins `maxPollAttempts x pollIntervalMs >= executionDeadlineMs` so the request budget can never be what silently ends the wait first, and both give-up paths cancel so no path walks away from a live execution. WHAT THE DEFAULT IS WORTH IN CREDITS, because a lane's budget is sized from it: at the measured 180.002 credits per 30-minute timeout - ~6.0 credits an engine-minute, an INFERENCE from one reading and not a published rate - 120 s is at most 13 credits of compute (client.mjs -> executionDeadlineCredits, whole credits rounded up). CONDITIONALLY: cancelling bounds the WAIT for certain and the BILL only if Dune stops the engine on cancel, which the vendor does not document and settling would cost a deliberately-runaway execution. That is why `worstCaseCreditsPerExecution` stays at the ENGINE floor of 200 rather than dropping to 13 - the pin is honest under either answer, and the deadline is what makes 13 the expected worst case instead of 200. WHY 120 s IS CONSERVATIVE RATHER THAN TIGHT: it is 1/15 of the engine limit and >13x the longest Dune execution this repository has measured (6-9 s for these two queries, 2026-08-03). It governs every execution this leg issues, the coverage probe's refresh included. It is pinned EQUAL to the census's for one reason and it is not tidiness: both keyed lanes read the same account, so an operator sizing a month has one deadline to reason about rather than two.
justification.resultBytesPerRowCeiling: 121 bytes per result row, UNCHANGED at SIX columns and, for the first time, backed by a measurement of the production shape rather than by arithmetic over an unobserved column. It is pinned here because the credit guard needs it as a number, and a bound that exists only in a sentence cannot be arithmetic. HISTORY: measured 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns, ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes); the fifth, launches_total, was then bounded by ARITHMETIC at <=24 bytes, and that is where 121 came from. CAPTAIN DECISION 227a ADDS A SIXTH, is_mayhem_mode, so this ceiling was RE-MEASURED rather than assumed to survive it — 2026-08-05, through enumerateCreations against the deployed query: 51,691 bytes over 488 rows in the same five-wallet batch shape = 105.92 bytes/row, and 26,690 bytes over 252 rows for ONE wallet = 105.91. Both sit under 121, so the pinned value DOES NOT MOVE. TWO THINGS THE RE-MEASUREMENT CHANGED THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE NUMBER. (1) The two shapes agree to two decimals, so total_result_set_bytes is per-row with negligible per-response overhead at these sizes — which CONTRADICTS the stated cause of the older ~115 bytes/row five-column reading (28,699 bytes over 250 rows, one wallet), which this file attributed to overhead amortised over fewer rows. A 252-row read now lands at the same figure as a 488-row one, so that explanation does not hold, the 115 does not reproduce in this accounting, and it must not be carried forward. (2) THE HEADROOM IS NOW THINNER THAN ONE MORE COLUMN IS WORTH: 121 - 105.92 = 15.08 bytes, against an arithmetic worst case of ~23 for a single boolean column (a JSON key plus `false`). So this ceiling survives the sixth column and would NOT survive a seventh by arithmetic. A SEVENTH COLUMN MUST RE-MEASURE AND RAISE THIS VALUE rather than lean on a margin that is no longer there. It bounds the EXPORT half of the worst case: maxResultRows x this x (maxExecutionsPerRun + 1) reads at 20 credits/MB. RAISING maxResultRows OR ADDING A COLUMN MOVES THIS, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c owns every figure above.
justification.allowanceReserveCredits: 25 credits held back from every allowance reading before the plan is compared against it, and it exists because THE COUNTER LAGS. Measured on this account during the Dune evaluation: `credits_used` rose +6.0 while the evaluator was completely idle, and it lands in whole-credit jumps — so a reading understates spend, therefore OVERSTATES what remains, and a guard that spent to the last credit would be spending money the vendor has already taken. It also absorbs part of a second gap it cannot measure, and the key being UNSHARED does not close it: the allowance is ONE ACCOUNT's, every lane and run of this fleet draws on the same account total, nothing tracks it between runs, so a sibling lane can spend between our reading and our execution — and a SEPARATE key is a separate account with its own quota and its own period, which a reading says nothing about. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE and it is stated rather than dressed up: 25 is ~4x the single observed drift and 1% of the free tier's 2,500. What would justify a value: a series of readings taken immediately before and after executions of known cost, which would price the lag distribution instead of one sample of it. The failure direction is the safe one — too large a reserve refuses a run that would have fitted, and this leg's refusal falls back to the RPC walk, which is slower rather than wrong.
justification.allowanceTightMultiple: 2. NOT A REFUSAL BAR — the threshold at which a run that WILL proceed prints a warning. A run whose worst case fits once but not twice may be the last one the period can afford, and an operator queueing heavier work behind it should learn that before the allowance is gone rather than from an HTTP 402 mid-run. NO MEASUREMENT BACKS THE 2, and here is what would: the distribution of Dune-spending runs per billing period, which does not exist because nothing here has yet run on a schedule. 2 is chosen as the smallest multiple that expresses 'this run is repeatable', which is the property that makes a failure recoverable.
justification.allowanceRequired: `true` — a run REFUSES the whole Dune leg when POST /usage cannot be read, rather than proceeding blind. NOT A MEASUREMENT, a policy, and it is the one the whole guard turns on: an unreadable balance is not headroom, and 'we could not see it' is the same evidence as 'it is empty'. The cost of being wrong is bounded and known — this leg falls back to the Solana RPC walk, which needs no Dune credential and is slower rather than wrong — while the cost of being wrong the other way is a billed multi-execution run that dies partway with neither a result nor the credits to retry. The reading itself is free (Dune documents /usage as a metadata endpoint consuming no credits) and is retried once, so a single transport hiccup does not reach this switch.
justification.legFallbackHealthyWalkShare: 0.133 — the share of a batch a HEALTHY Dune leg still sends to the creation walk, and the whole point of pinning it is that the baseline a spend cliff is measured against must be the plan that was actually made rather than zero. MEASURED, from records committed in this repository rather than from a report held elsewhere: the two legs of tools/deployer-screen/measurements/2026-08-05-seed-comparison/ whose Dune leg ANSWERED refused 6 of 69 candidates per wallet (good) and 11 of 59 (elite) — a coverage probe turns down one wallet at a time — which is 17 of 128 pooled = 0.1328. WHAT IT IS NOT: this is not a failure rate and not a forecast. It is the denominator of the multiple below, and using the run's OWN answered count instead is impossible by construction, because the case this guard fires in is the one where that count is zero. LIMITS, stated rather than dressed up: n = 2 runs, one day, one vendor's tier membership, and the two legs disagree by 2x (0.087 and 0.186), so the pooled figure is a point estimate with no interval. It moves the guard's crossover and nothing else — no bar, no verdict and no measured value reads it. What would justify a value: the same share over a series of runs across weeks, which does not exist because nothing here has yet run on a schedule. THE FAILURE DIRECTION IS THE SAFE ONE: too LARGE a share raises the baseline and makes the guard quieter, so it errs towards letting a run proceed, which is the side where the walk still produces a correct measurement.
justification.legFallbackCliffMultiple: 4x. The multiple by which a WHOLE-BATCH Dune fallback may raise this run's enumeration worst case before screen.mjs refuses to continue without --allow-walk-fallback. Captain decision 298a, 2026-08-06. WHAT IT COMPARES, and both sides are one expression evaluated twice with only the candidate count changed: the projection is every candidate walking, the baseline is legFallbackHealthyWalkShare of them walking, and both are priced at the same per-candidate ceiling (creation_walk_helius.maxCreditsPerCandidate with a Helius key, creation_walk.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate without one), so the unit cancels and the multiple is a ratio of candidate counts. dune.mjs -> priceWalkFallbackCliff owns the arithmetic. WHY A GUARD AT ALL: the Dune path is primary (captain decision 156a) and roughly two orders of magnitude cheaper per candidate than its own fallback, so losing it is a CLIFF and not a gradient — measured, in this repository: 232,937 Helius credits over 76 candidates on the 2026-08-05 untiered leg that lost its Dune answer, against 1,924 over 69 and 21,733 over 59 for the two legs that kept theirs, and 221,731 credits with 3,941 RPC requests on runs/2026-08-04.json, whose whole leg died on a failed coverage-probe execution. creation_walk_helius.maxCreditsPerRun does NOT fire on any of them and cannot: it is sized for the walk being the INTENDED route, so it already reserves every candidate walking. WHY 4 AND NOT ANOTHER NUMBER: at the pinned share the whole-batch multiple is 1 / 0.133 = 7.5x pooled, and 11.5x and 5.4x on the two measured legs read apart. 4 sits BELOW the smaller of those two, so the guard fires on every population this repository has measured, and it is the largest round value that does — 6 would clear 5.4 by too little to survive one more elite-shaped leg. IT IS NOT A CONSTANT DESPITE THE RATIO BEING SCALE-FREE: the baseline rounds UP to at least one candidate, so a batch of 8 or fewer is at most 4x and proceeds, and the guard first bites at 9 candidates (4.5x, ~46,800 Helius credits worst case). A cliff is a magnitude as well as a ratio, and a run small enough that the share rounds up to half of it has not fallen off one. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it never distrusts the walk, which is the correct answer to a Dune refusal and the only surface that can say who holds a curve today. It refuses to take a thousand-fold spend decision SILENTLY on a plan approved for a different route, and --allow-walk-fallback is how an operator takes it deliberately. It also does not fire on a run that never asked Dune — no key, --no-dune or --ownership-only — because there the walk is the route that was planned.
justification.legFallbackMinCandidates: 9 candidates. The MAGNITUDE floor under the guard above: a whole-batch Dune fallback on a batch smaller than this is never refused, whatever its ratio reads. Captain decision 308a, 2026-08-06. NO NEW ANCHOR ENTERS THE REPOSITORY WITH IT — 9 is exactly the number legFallbackCliffMultiple's own justification already publishes ('a batch of 8 or fewer is at most 4x and proceeds, and the guard first bites at 9 candidates (4.5x, ~46,800 Helius credits worst case)'), and this key does nothing but make the code true to that sentence instead of leaving it to be implied. WHY IT HAD TO BE WRITTEN DOWN: the baseline rounds UP to a whole candidate, so the multiple moves in bands, and those bands are NOT monotone at the bottom — at share 0.133 a batch of 5, 6 or 7 reads 5.0x, 6.0x and 7.0x and would fire, while a batch of 8 reads exactly 4.0x and would not, so a run worth ~26,000 Helius credits would be refused while one worth ~41,600 proceeded. That is indefensible on the guard's own magnitude argument. MONOTONICITY IS THE PROPERTY IT BUYS, and it is asserted by a test rather than argued here: from 9 up the smallest multiple in each band is 16/3, 23/4, 31/5 and so on, rising towards 1 / 0.133 = 7.5, so once the guard fires it fires on every larger batch. LIMITS: it inherits legFallbackCliffMultiple's evidence and adds none of its own — n = 2 runs, one day — and it moves the crossover only. THE FAILURE DIRECTION IS THE SAFE ONE: too HIGH a floor lets a small degraded run proceed, which spends at most 8 candidates' worth of walk and still produces a correct measurement.
justification.refreshProbeByDefault: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch, and it is `false` because the probe is PARAMETERLESS and therefore has a cached answer that costs no execution at all. Re-executing it every run would spend the binding budget on a figure that moves by one row per second. `--dune-refresh-probe` makes it explicit, and staleness re-executes it anyway (see maxCoverageLagMs), so the default cannot silently publish a count over coverage nobody checked.

stage0.subjectVerdictMeaning: The gate PASSES our subject deployer, whose opening window is known to be unprofitable for outsiders since 2026-06-04. Passing this gate does not mean a deployer is worth the time.

knownNegativeControl.meaning: Stage 2 must NOT score this wallet as having entry room. It is competent (the gate passes it) and it is not beatable — measured in analysis/window-population/README.md §4.1 and §4.3 over the committed tape, and asserted by test/window-population.test.ts, not assumed. Note that the field leg, gross of fees, says the opposite: a verdict that follows it would be wrong, which is why the field can only veto and never pass.

limitations: WHAT THIS IS: a candidate list for further research. Nothing here is a recommendation, and
nothing here establishes a tradeable edge.
WHAT IT MEASURES:
· STAGE 1, competence — whether a deployer's tokens RAISE. The measure is RAISE-85 (captain
decision 352b): net quote inflow into a token's own primary market, over its first 24 hours,
reaching 85 SOL-equivalent — the same bar on every venue, pump.fun included, replacing
pump.fun's own graduation flag as the definition. One number, computed by us from per-token
records. Every route this tool has today READS that criterion through pump.fun's graduation
flag, which is an estimator of it whose positive is an upper bound, so a rate here errs
towards acceptance and the candidate row says how much of it was estimated.
· STAGE 2, ENTRY — how much of its own opening window the deployer and its own wallets take
before anyone else is filled, and what the OTHER sniping wallets on those same launches
achieved: fill, queue position, and realised P&L. Distributions and a hit rate, never a mean.
· STAGE 2, THE PRICE OF THE SEAT — what landing in that window cost those wallets, recovered
from the chain: the transaction fee (base and priority) exactly, and everything else their
own transaction moved. The field's result is then reported both gross and NET of it.
WHICH HISTORY IT COUNTS: the tokens the wallet CREATED, read from pump.fun create transactions.
NOT the tokens it owns now, which is what every vendor surface answers. Ownership on pump.fun
is a sellable position — the owner collects the creator fees — so the ownership reading
understates launches, understates BONDED launches by more, and scores the better deployer
worse. Both readings are in every candidate row, with the verdict each one produced.
The creation walk covers a BOUNDED WINDOW backwards from now; outside it the ownership listing
is carried over unchanged and the row says how much of the history that is.
WHAT IT DOES NOT MEASURE, and none of these are minor:
· WHETHER ONE BAR MEANS THE SAME THING ON TWO VENUES. EQUIVALENT STRICTNESS ACROSS VENUES IS NOT
ESTABLISHED: the same 85-SOL bar is reached by 0.80% of new pump.fun tokens, 0.25% on Meteora
DBC and 46.71% on Meteora CPAMM, and nothing measured here separates a venue that attracts
more capital per token from a venue whose tokens are counted differently. One bar applied
identically everywhere is what 352b adopts; cross-venue COMPARABILITY is not claimed by it and
must not be claimed from it. (slot-zero-cross-venue-strictness-measure owns the question; it
is held in firstmate's records, not in this repo.)
· EXIT. Room to enter is not room to leave. When the dev sells, whether its trigger is a SIZE
that our own buy would count towards and would therefore cap our position, and whether an
outsider could have got out first, are ALL UNMEASURED here. No exit signal reaches any entry
number in this output, deliberately: a blended score cannot be read back apart.
· A LANDING TIP PAID IN A SEPARATE TRANSACTION OF THE SAME BUNDLE. It is not recoverable from
the entrant's own transaction and it is not measured anywhere in this repo's ground truth
either, so every cost figure is a LOWER bound and every after-cost figure an UPPER bound:
entry looks cheaper, and the field more profitable, than either was.
· WHETHER WE WOULD HAVE BEEN FILLED AT ALL. Every fill in the tape belongs to a wallet that
WON the auction — post-break our own subject saw a median 41.6 attempts per landed
transaction — and a wallet that paid and did not land is invisible to it. So the measured
cost of entering is the cost paid by winners and it understates the cost of TRYING.
· Lead time, or the independence of the actors involved.
The standing bar for acting on a signal of this class is real lead time, independence of the
